💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around 265,000 customers potentially affected as London transport operator grapples with another security breach.
  • Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.
  • In a recent development, the capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around 265,000 customers potentially affected as London transport operator grapples with another security breach.

Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

In a recent development, the capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

"We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," noted Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident.".

According to recent reports, tfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.

In a recent development, tfL indicates no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL notes it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

Recent findings suggest that tfL notes it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

Sources indicate that existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.

"We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma stated.

TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.

Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®.

Breaking: Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories.
  • Industry observers note that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge.
  • Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Industry observers note that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

In a recent development, A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

Both systems refuse to compress.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

It has been revealed that we reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

According to recent reports, consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:.

Sources indicate that on the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Recent findings suggest that where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:.

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

Recent findings suggest that the two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

According to recent reports, we give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.).

It has been revealed that both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

Sources indicate that appWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister calls notification delay 'not acceptable' after October attack on Irish banking player Wellington IT came to light in November.

An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the firm's delay in notifying them.

Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, noted the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.

Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable.".

News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.

It has been revealed that affected credit unions noted attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.

Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.

The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.

The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:.

Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames.

Business Identifier Codes (BICs).

International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs).

Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers.

Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.

Industry observers note that st. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.

The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, mentioned in a statement that the manufacturer notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data.".

He remarked Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

It has been revealed that "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses.".

Owned by Canadian manufacturer Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.

Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said.

Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.

Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.

"What's most crucial is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said.

Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday.

The FCA remarked October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing upcoming rules. ®.

  • OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models.
  • Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth.

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for consumers of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Industry observers note that computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:.

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Recent findings suggest that studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Industry observers note that because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

Recent findings suggest that the examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

Sources indicate that this query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Sources indicate that similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates rapidly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:.

It has been revealed that this is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

It has been revealed that sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

According to recent reports, flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

In a recent development, similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

In a recent development, custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

According to recent reports, while we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

It has been revealed that A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

This article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

Industry observers note that for this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

It has been revealed that image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Recent findings suggest that whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

Sources indicate that give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

Sources indicate that after generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

Record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

Recent findings suggest that glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

Run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:.

In a recent development, when an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

Load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below highlights the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

Industry observers note that the alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

Sources indicate that A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

The same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

The audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

In a recent development, inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

It has been revealed that decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

According to recent reports, do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

When should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

Is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

How can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

With my implementation, you will be able to do it!

The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way.

We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of elements inside it.

And the container controls the variables of :nth-child():.

I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow.

Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element:.

I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected.

We can translate this into the following CSS code:.

Industry observers note that I am using the newly introduced if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style(). If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens.

The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows:.

The tricky part is how to define the condition within style(). I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if().” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works. From there, you will notice that our condition can be written several ways that are all valid:.

Sources indicate that the code looks a bit redundant, which is probably one of the drawbacks of this method, but it’s still cool to implement the selector and be able to adjust the value of --B on the fly. Don’t forget that our goal is to learn fresh tricks, and you already have two of them in your pocket (sibling-index() and if()).

Here is an interactive demo where you can adjust the value of --B and see the changes:.

Let’s move to our next selector. It selects more than one element.

Think for a moment about how to implement such a selector. It’s almost the same as the previous one.

In a recent development, if the index of the element is greater than or equal to the value of --B, the element is selected. As simple as that!

Sources indicate that what about this one? Easy, right? We simply use <= instead of >=!

We can also easily implement a range selection, which is the combination of both selectors:.

Sources indicate that the code should be self-explanatory. It’s even more intuitive than the :nth-child() notation, which requires a few minutes of deciphering if you are not used to it.

It has been revealed that now let’s deal with the A argument. For example, the following selector:.

…selects the 3rd, 6th, 9th, etc. elements. Seen differently, the index of the element needs to be a multiple of 3. To do such testing, we can use the mod() function. If mod(index, 3) returns 0, it means the remainder of the division of index by 3 is equal to 0, hence, it’s a multiple of 3.

Recent findings suggest that it works! Another selector with a simple implementation.

We can identify two special cases. When --A is equal to 1, we have :nth-child(n), which selects all the elements and when it’s equal to 2, we have :nth-child(2n) which is also :nth-child(even).

According to recent reports, while this works fine, there is a small gotcha. When A is a negative value, the selector should select nothing which is logical as all the indexes are positive, but if you try using negative values with my implementation, some elements still get selected which is wrong.

The mod() function works with negative numbers and can still return 0 in such cases, so to be more accurate, we should test the sign of A.

According to recent reports, see that? I simply added another condition inside style() using the and keyword. The syntax of if() may sound confusing at first glance, but at the end it’s the same as any other language: a bunch of conditions defined inside style(). You can have as many as you want combined with and and or.

Now, our selection is more precise.

Now let’s combine all the tricks we learned so far to implement the generic form of :nth-child(). In this case, the index is equal to An + B, and we can express n like this:.

According to recent reports, n should be a positive integer (zero included). For the positive part, we can use:.

For the integer part, we need to make sure index - B is a multiple of A, and for this, we use mod():.

We translate this into CSS to get the following:.

Recent findings suggest that we are almost good except for the case when --A is equal to 0. In that case, the selection is simply wrong. The mod() results in NaN since its second argument is equal to 0, and this will mess with the condition. Actually, that condition is not meant to work with --A equal to 0.

We either consider that this implementation is only valid for a value of --A different from 0 (which is probably what we want) or we try to find a solution to include that case.

We are here to learn and discover newly introduced stuff, so let’s try something else. There are probably a lot of ways to fix the case of 0, but here is my idea:.

Recent findings suggest that as you can see, I have introduced a upcoming variable that should be equal to 1 if the element is selected by :nth-child(An + B). Try to dissect the code to understand how it works. If you still struggle, check the following post: “Dynamic nth-child() using sibling-index() andif().”.

And here is the final interactive with the complete implementation of :nth-child(An + B):.

#46842. What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

📅 13 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2255 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

📅 13 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim.
  • In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.
  • Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯.

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:.

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully.".

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Industry observers note that rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:.

According to recent reports, participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:.

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:.

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:.

It has been revealed that 51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

Industry observers note that 23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:.

Recent findings suggest that 35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:.

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Sources indicate that theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

Industry observers note that an evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

Recent findings suggest that 🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

Sources indicate that we have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:.

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a upcoming arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗.

Recent findings suggest that the most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:.

It has been revealed that pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

According to recent reports, some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics noted "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check.".

Industry observers note that so what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

Sources indicate that to the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗.

According to recent reports, it was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing crucial insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

I have been working on a complementary experiment at https://ReproducibleAIList.org, though not the same scale. We've been taking models from Chip Huyen's GoodAIList.com and having a clean-room agent try to reproduce each one from scratch using the code repos (not the papers).

One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.

It has been revealed that very cool, roar sounds like a great package! I'll take a look and see what we can learn from roar.

Really enjoyed being part of this experiment. Gratifying to see our reproduction highlighted as one of the community’s best.

“A Coin Flip for Safety” was reproduced using AlphaXiv’s OpenResearch with OpenCode’s free BigPickle model, with experiments run locally on 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090s.

It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.

Thanks to the Hugging Face and AlphaXiv teams for organizing the challenge and making the whole process open and reproducible!

Thanks to the Hugging Face and AlphaXiv teams for organizing the challenge and making the whole process open and reproducible!

In a recent development, really enjoyed being part of this experiment. Gratifying to see our reproduction highlighted as one of the community’s best.“A Coin Flip for Safety” was reproduced using AlphaXiv’s OpenResearch with OpenCode’s free BigPickle model, with experiments run locally on 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090s.It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.Thanks to the Hugging Face and AlphaXiv teams for organizing the challenge and making the whole process open and reproducible!One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us bilibili the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing key insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

According to recent reports, the scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days reveals how rapidly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻.

According to recent reports, what I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊.

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly vital... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️.

Most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apps retire in June 2027, with no automatic task migration and no Planner replacement for personal accounts.
  • Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.
  • According to recent reports, the confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and looks for Copilot and Microsoft 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apps retire in June 2027, with no automatic task migration and no Planner replacement for personal accounts.

Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

According to recent reports, the confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and looks for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the organization's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private strategy, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

According to recent reports, existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out.".

Sources indicate that unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier.".

Some customers responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent.".

It has been revealed that indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.

Industry observers note that the message for To Do consumers appears to be: Get with the Initiative(ner) or just get out. ®.
